sn12.38:1.2: “Intend” (_ceteti_) and “plan” (_pakappeti_) play the role of “choices” (_saṅkhāra_), while “underlying tendencies” (_anuseti_) stand for “ignorance”. | This Sutta illustrates the threefold pattern (_tivaṭṭa_) into which dependent origination was later analyzed. The twelve factors are grouped under three headings: ignorance, craving, and grasping are “defilements” (_kilesavaṭṭa_); choices and continued existence are “deeds” (_kammavaṭṭa_); the remainder are “results” (_vipākavaṭṭa_). Within these groups we find different synonyms or related terms are used in particular contexts (see eg. [sn12.19]()). The least fitting in this scheme is _bhava_, which includes all three, but is counted under “deeds” here as it connects grasping with rebirth. We find this pattern expressed in different ways elsewhere in the suttas; for example, [sn46.26:2.2]() says that due to practicing the awakening factors, craving is given up (_kilesavaṭṭa_), then deeds (_kammavaṭṭa_), then suffering (_vipākavaṭṭa_).
sn12.38:1.3: That is, it takes rebirth in a new life.
sn12.38:1.4: It “grows” as the individual grows up and matures, leading to renewal of the cycle (see [sn12.64](), [sn22.53](), [mn38:28.1]()).
sn12.38:2.1: Underlying tendencies manifest as morally potent choices. But we usually don’t make such choices continually; they only occur from time to time. Much of the time there is no active volition, for example, when we are asleep. But so long as the tendencies are still there, one is not freed.
